Someone has already posted "ssh". I'll say that it's still the answer, but assume some explanation would be helpful.

Security is hard, really really hard, everyone makes horrific mistakes type of hard. Ssh is intentionally rather plain. Sure it can do fancy things across a network, but network access is to be expected for remote access. I would hope that anyone working on ssh is good at writing network code. But that is about it, it does network, some more network fancy things, and plainly sends data to a program of your choosing. The default is to start a console, the simple typeity-type screen. I know not everyone is well practiced at that, but it's only the default. It's just as capable of starting a VNC session (remote desktop), starting a movie player, pretty much starting any program and sending data to it. SSH is the most common means of accessing a remote machine running Linux for a reason, it's security track record is impressive. A few rare options may have leaked some information and a vast number may have never been vulnerable ever. SSH using key files is just about bullet-proof.

I would say that figuring out how to at least start ssh is a requirement for any Linux work. Most likely ssh is also an option on the router, making remote access with one tool, easy and secure from anywhere.

An interesting app that can help you is Guacamole Server. It is a headless server that supports both RDP and VNC protocols. You can use an RDP client like reminna or even your Firefox browser to remotely control your desktop!
Vnc is pretty easy to setup. I use the x11 vnc server in the mint repo.
Xrdp sucks. Vnc sucks. Ssh is useful, but a real rdp alternative would be lovely.
